raw_output.question: Why does Kant argue that only morally good ends should be taught to children, rather than skills for arbitrary purposes?

key_points.statement: Kant says that imperatives of skill are about how to achieve any possible end, not about whether the end is good or rational.
key_points.quote: Here there is no question whether the end is rational and good, but only what one must do in order to attain it.
key_points.speaker: author_sincere

key_points.statement: He observes that parents teach children many skills for arbitrary ends, without judging whether those ends are valuable.
key_points.quote: parents seek to have their children taught a great many things, and provide for their skill in the use of means for all sorts of arbitrary ends, of none of which can they determine whether it may not perhaps hereafter be an object to their pupil
key_points.speaker: author_sincere

raw_output.premise: Kant believes that only morally good ends should be taught to children, not skills for arbitrary purposes.
